seoDescription: Explore the key updates in Svelte 4, a maintenance release designed as a stepping stone to Svelte 5. This video breaks down the most significant changes, including a 75% reduction in package size for faster installs, improved performance, and major enhancements to the developer experience. Learn about the improved IDE integration, which fixes auto-import and "go to definition" issues, and understand why the Svelte codebase shifted from TypeScript to JSDoc for better library maintainability.

chapters.title: Introducing Svelte 4: New Website & Tutorial
chapters.description: Explore the brand new Svelte 4 website, its improved documentation and REPL, and the powerful in-browser tutorial powered by WebContainers.

chapters.title: A Performance-Focused Maintenance Release
chapters.description: Learn why Svelte 4 is primarily a maintenance release focused on modernizing the codebase, reducing package size by 75%, and preparing for Svelte 5.

chapters.title: Key Changes: Local Transitions and Web Components
chapters.description: Discover how Svelte 4 makes transitions 'local' by default to fix bugs and overhauls the custom element implementation for web components.

chapters.title: A Better Developer Experience: IDE Improvements
chapters.description: See how Svelte 4 vastly improves the IDE experience by fixing auto-imports and go-to-definition behavior, thanks to the dts-buddy package.

chapters.title: Rich Harris on TypeScript vs. JSDoc
chapters.description: Rich Harris explains the rationale behind moving the Svelte codebase from TypeScript files to JSDoc annotations to reduce development friction for a library.

chapters.title: Why Svelte's Codebase Moved to JSDoc
chapters.description: This section clarifies that the move to JSDoc is an internal tooling choice and does not prevent you from using TypeScript in your Svelte apps.

chapters.title: Migration Guide: Breaking Changes & New Features
chapters.description: A walkthrough of the official migration guide, including the new Node.js 16 requirement, stricter types, and the ability to iterate over any iterable in `each` blocks.

chapters.title: The Future is Bright: Svelte 5 and the Growing Team
chapters.description: Learn about the upcoming Svelte 5 rewrite and the expansion of the full-time Svelte team at Vercel, including high-profile hire Dominic Gannaway.

chapters.title: Outro & Support
chapters.description: The video concludes with a call to action to upgrade, subscribe, and support the creator's work.

summary:
## Svelte 4: A Maintenance Release

Svelte 4 is not a major feature release, but a crucial **maintenance and modernization update**. Its primary goal is to prepare the groundwork for the upcoming rewrite in Svelte 5.

- It's smaller, faster, and provides a better developer experience.
- The minimum required Node.js version is now **Node 16**.

## Key Performance Improvements

- **Package Size:** The `svelte` package has been reduced by nearly **75%**, from ~10.6 MB to ~2.8 MB.
- **Benefits:** This leads to faster `npm install` times and quicker startup for tools like the Svelte REPL.

## Major Feature Updates

- **Transitions:** Transitions are now `local` by default, which prevents animations from playing incorrectly when a parent element is removed, a common issue with page transitions.

- **Web Components:** The way Svelte generates custom elements has been completely overhauled, fixing a class of bugs and improving consistency. The old `tag` option is deprecated in favor of a new `customElement` option.

- **`each` Blocks:** You can now iterate over any **iterable** (like `Set` or `Map`) inside an `{#each}` block, not just arrays.

> [!TIP]
The new default 'local' transitions simplify creating smooth page navigations in SvelteKit without needing to manually add the `local` directive to every transition.

## Improved Developer Experience (DX)

Svelte 4 provides significant quality-of-life improvements for developers in their code editors.

- **Better Auto-Import:** The IDE will no longer suggest incorrect imports from Svelte's internal files.
- **Smarter "Go to Definition":** Navigating to a function's definition now takes you to the actual JavaScript source code, not the TypeScript type declaration (`.d.ts`) file.

> [!NOTE]
> These improvements are powered by a new package called `dts-buddy` and are available in any editor that uses the Svelte Language Server, including VS Code and Vim.

## The TypeScript to JSDoc Switch

Svelte's internal codebase was migrated from using TypeScript (`.ts`) files to using JavaScript with **JSDoc comments** for types.

- **Reasoning:** For **library development**, using TypeScript files introduces a mandatory compilation step that creates friction. JSDoc allows the team to get full type-safety without this build-step overhead, enabling them to move faster.
- **Rich Harris's View:** "Types are fantastic, TypeScript is a bit of a pain."

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This is an **internal tooling decision** for the Svelte library itself. It does **not** affect end-users. You can and should continue to use TypeScript in your Svelte and SvelteKit applications as you always have.

## Looking Ahead: Svelte 5

- **The Next Generation:** Svelte 5 will be a complete rewrite of the compiler and runtime, promising major advancements.
- **A Fully-Funded Team:** With investment from Vercel, the Svelte team now includes three full-time maintainers:
  - **Rich Harris** (Creator of Svelte)
  - **Simon**
  - **Dominic Gannaway** (Creator of InfernoJS)
transcription:
## Introducing Svelte 4: New Website & Tutorial

Hey friends. We're going to talk about the new version of Svelte that just got released, which is Svelte 4. So I hope you have your coffee ready and let's go. Ah, beautiful.

So Svelte 4 just got released and is sporting a new site which looks absolutely beautiful. It has a new documentation which is not a single page application anymore. Now we even have a search and this is really awesome. The Svelte REPL also got updated to CodeMirror 6.

And then of course, the best part in my opinion is the Svelte tutorial. And if you didn't know, this uses WebContainer, which is a new technology that lets you run Node in the browser. So not only can you learn Svelte—so you have here basic Svelte, advanced Svelte—you can learn SvelteKit in the browser. So you can go from basic SvelteKit to advanced SvelteKit. And of course, all of these links are going to be in the description. Alright, so let's look at the announcement.

## A Performance-Focused Maintenance Release

So here is the announcement for Svelte 4. So as they say here, time flies. Svelte 3 was released more than four years ago. Wow. As they say, that's eons in JavaScript framework time. But honestly, Svelte, it's so great they didn't even have to improve a lot of things. But things are changing now, and basically Svelte 4 is just a stepping stone towards Svelte 5.

So as they say, Svelte 4 is mainly a maintenance release. The goal was to modernize the codebase so it's easier to go from Svelte 4 to Svelte 5. But that doesn't mean there's no features, because there's a lot of cool features I want to talk about, and some changes including the goofy TypeScript drama when Svelte changed from TypeScript to JSDoc. So we're going to also talk about that. And let's go for this post.

So let me just see what's new. So, performance: they reduced the bundle size. Since you don't have to support a lot of legacy things, you can see Svelte 4 reduces the Svelte package size by nearly 75%. So the Svelte package size went from 10 megabytes to almost 3 megabytes. And this is really awesome for install times, the REPL, how fast you need to boot up, and etc. As you can see here for the site where they use it, they say they reduced the size by 12%.

## Key Changes: Local Transitions and Web Components

So, another awesome thing is that `local` is Now the default for transition. So if you ever use page transitions, then you probably encounter some weird behavior animations because animations are going to play when the parent gets destroyed or removed. So basically, you had to use `local`, which is default now, as I think it should be, and it's going to eliminate a lot of problems, and that's really awesome.

Then there's news for you web components lovers. I unfortunately don't use web components, so I really don't know how great this is, but apparently a lot of people are excited about this. So for users of web components, the largest change is an overhaul of the way Svelte authors custom elements. So they change how they're generated which eliminates a whole class of bugs and inconsistencies. And if you're excited about web components, then this news is going to be awesome for you.

## A Better Developer Experience: IDE Improvements

This is one of my favorite changes. They made several improvements to the IDE authoring experience. So I'm not sure about you, but how many times have you tried to use the auto-import in VS Code and it would import some random junk from, I don't know, some internals or etc. Or there's this annoying thing with TypeScript, you just want to go to the code definition, maybe you want to learn how something works, but when you press Alt or whatever your key is, it leads you to the type definition. You're like, okay, this sucks.

Well, this experience has been greatly improved thanks to this package that Rich Harris made. So he made this DTS-buddy package and basically it fixes type declarations and all these sort of things like imports. As he says, it provides with the better type declarations in the smaller package. So let's actually see this in action.

So you can see here `onMount`, you will do something like this and it will give you always this goofy import. Exactly. Even... I love Rich. Okay, so this is the problem they're talking about. So you want to just check the function, what it does. You know, okay, where am I? Especially if you don't understand TypeScript or use that material. Okay, what is even this DTS file? You can see here the import is goofy. When you want to import this `fade`, then you're like, your tooling basically fails you, right? And also this funny thing where it includes the extension and then like JS or TS. So basically, that has been resolved.

And now let's look at the updated version. So now, as you can see, let's try this again. `onMount`. Good, it does exactly what you expect it to. Good job VS Code. Of course, this isn't specific to VS Code. The Svelte Language Server can be used in any editor, so everyone benefits, even if you're using VS Code or Vim. As you can see, how awesome is this? You can actually go into the internals and learn how this works. As I said, some people think that Svelte being a compiler is this intimidating thing, but as you can see here is how simple animation is implemented in Svelte. Look like, and then you can learn about things like this. And this is really awesome in my opinion.

## Rich Harris on TypeScript vs. JSDoc

But let's also talk about the goofy TypeScript drama. So many people made a deal out of it for nothing. So instead of me telling you why they made that transition from TypeScript to JSDoc, let Rich tell you:

Basically, my position is types are fantastic, TypeScript is a bit of a pain. And what I mean by that is types are great because you get type checking, obviously, prevention of buggy code, you get IntelliSense, you get autocomplete, and if you hover over something in your IDE it will show you inline documentation. Uh, there's all these really tremendous benefits of using types in your codebase. But as soon as you use TypeScript, by which I mean a `.ts` file, then you need tooling to support that. Um, in particular, if you're building a library in TypeScript and you're using that library in a separate project, you can't just kind of go into your node modules and fiddle around with the code base and expect it to run. Like, you're going to have to rebuild the code and there's all these points of friction that get added when you use a non-standard language like TypeScript that I have come to believe makes it not worth it. So instead, we put our type annotations in JSDoc comments. So we get all the type safety but in the other direction because it's just JavaScript, everything's just in comments and so you just run the code. Um, and so this is what we do inside the SvelteKit code base and it's worked out fantastically. And for Svelte 4, we're going to do the same for Svelte itself because it's going to enable us to move much more quickly.

You've heard it.

## Why Svelte's Codebase Moved to JSDoc

So basically, as Rich says, okay, we really don't like the experience of TypeScript for making libraries, but it's really awesome if you're somewhere like a front-end developer that's not really working on a library. Because since you already have a build step, why not use TypeScript? But it really makes development for library maintainers harder, and basically that's all that it comes down to. If you didn't know, SvelteKit already used this approach, as Rich said. So I'm really confused when this was such a huge issue because people were like, oh, you can't use TypeScript. But they're not taking your TypeScript. They're still using TypeScript, but they're using it over JSDoc, right? And they generate the types and you have awesome type completion. So Svelte is not abandoning TypeScript, in fact, they're embracing it more. And the point of the change is to make their lives a lot easier.

And also, let me show you that. So here was the pull request, TS to JSDoc. So as you can see here, for example, I just talked about transitions. Here's a transition. So here you can see it still has a `.d.ts` extension, but now they're just stripped the interface and they replace it with JSDoc. And if you don't know what JSDoc is, basically this is JSDoc, this sort of comments in your code. They don't have a build step, which makes testing easier and etc. And yeah, this is really awesome for Svelte. So it lets them move quicker, and it really doesn't affect you as the end user.

## Migration Guide: Breaking Changes & New Features

And of course, there's a migration guide. So we can see here the minimum version of Node is now 16, so they can shed a lot of legacy things, which makes the bundle size a lot smaller.

They have some stricter types for Svelte functions. So again, the types are even better. And yeah, you can read through this if you want. So custom elements with Svelte, they overhauled it and significantly improved. So now the `tag` option is deprecated in favor of the new `customElement` option. So you can see this looks like this. And if you're excited about web components, then this is for you.

Then deprecated this thing, which isn't really important. Transitions are local by default, which is awesome. So the default slot binding is no longer exposed to named slots. This isn't something you have to concern yourself about, but basically here you can bind props from slots to the parent component you can use it. And before it was bound by default in named slots like this, which is no longer the case anymore.

The preprocessor also got some changes, and now they're executed in order, so it's really easier to work with them. Then you have some other breaking changes. And then there's also these change logs you can read. So as I said, the minimum supported Node version is going to be Node 16. Let me look at some other things. So they overhauled and drastically improved creating custom elements with Svelte. They made transitions local to prevent confusion around page navigations. They also made some great changes they didn't mention in other places. Like for example, now when you use the custom store, you need to pass the `update` function and a `set` function, which avoids a lot of bugs and etc.

And we already talked about the not exposed default slot bindings to named slot and vice versa, so they change that. They change the order image preprocessors are applied. So this is one they didn't mention which is really awesome. Now inside of an each block, you can iterate over any iterable like Set, Map, and etc. And this is really awesome. And let me see if there's anything else. So we talked about generating type declarations with DTS-buddy so now that's going to be even more awesome. And you can go and read through all these changes if you want. But yeah, that's awesome.

## The Future is Bright: Svelte 5 and the Growing Team

So now let's go to the rest of the announcement. So as you can see, it's about the developer experience as we talked about, which is really awesome. So what is the future of Svelte? So Svelte 5 is going to be the next generation of Svelte. Svelte 5 will be a complete rewrite of the Svelte compiler and runtime. And as they said in this post, Svelte 4 was mainly about setting the ground for these future improvements by adopting modern tooling and dropping support for some legacy versions of various technologies. So the future of Svelte is really exciting.

And speaking about the future of Svelte, if you didn't know at this point, there are actually three full-time positions for people working on Svelte at Vercel. And people have this misconception that Vercel owns Svelte, but that's false. Vercel just pays the maintainers to work on Svelte and SvelteKit. It's really a symbiotic relationship because Vercel can test their platform features or whatever and make sure that SvelteKit and Svelte is the best experience on their platform. So they're really investing into the future of Svelte. Rich Harris already works at Vercel. Then the other person that was at Vercel was Simon, which is really awesome. But the new addition to the Svelte team is Dominic Gannaway, and this is an absolute mad lad. So he made LexicalJS and InfernoJS, and basically instead of me talking about it, let's hear Rich talk about what the monster Dominic is.

We could possibly compete against a competitive approach, right? It's compiling into all this clever signaling stuff. And Dominic just actually built this little minimal Inferno which demolished everything else, um, and that's because like he knows his way around the browser internals.

And yeah, you can imagine what the monster Svelte 5 is going to be with all of these brains behind them and the backing of Vercel. So yeah, the future of Svelte is looking really exciting. I can't wait to see what they're going to come up with Svelte 5 for reference.

## Outro & Support

So that's it. You can upgrade to Svelte 4 today. Don't forget to like and subscribe. If you want to support my work, you can become a patron. And you can also join the Discord server. Thank you for watching and catch you in the next one. Peace.
